newsitem.title: CANADA: Quebec biker war sparks outrage, pleas to Ottawa.
newsitem.headline: Quebec biker war sparks outrage, pleas to Ottawa.

text.p: The resurgence of a bloody turf war between rival motorcycle gangs that has killed 36 people in Quebec over the past three years is sparking growing public outrage and calls for government action.

Since the battle between the Hell's Angels and Rock Machine biker groups erupted in mid-1994, 88 bombs have been placed or exploded outside bars, restaurants and clubhouses connected to warring gang members, wreaking havoc in the French-speaking province of 7.3 million people.

At stake in the conflict is control of Quebec's lucrative trade in illegal drugs and contraband alcohol and cigarettes. Caught in the middle are terrified citizens worried that they might be maimed or killed by the next bomb or bullet intended for a rival gang member.
"We are in a state of crisis," said Quebec Public Security Minister Robert Perreault as the province urged Canada to introduce an anti-gang law.
After meeting with Quebec provincial and municipal officials on Thursday, Canadian Justice Minister Allan Rock promised to strengthen police powers to investigate gangs.
However, Rock said a sweeping anti-gang law favored by local politicians and police might run foul of Canada's Charter of Rights and be thrown out of court.
"That would be a cruel hoax for the families and for the citizens who are looking to us for hope and to restore tranquility," Rock said.

Most of the victims of the biker war have been known or suspected gang members. But Quebec was shocked by the August 1995 death in Montreal of 11-year-old Daniel Desrochers, who was killed by flying shrapnel from an exploding car bomb that police suspect was set by the Hell's Angels.
Several fatal bombings and shootings in the past few weeks have further outraged residents of Montreal, the province's biggest city, and Quebec City, its 389-year-old capital.
On Tuesday night, two men were killed in a Montreal suburb while trying to move a bomb placed outside a bar that police said was a suspected Hell's Angels hangout.

Last Sunday, 500 residents of Saint-Nicolas, a Quebec City suburb, marched peacefully on a fortified Hell's Angels bunker in a residential neighborhood, demanding that the bikers leave town. Masked and hooded Hell's Angels ominously filmed the gathering from the clubhouse rooftop.
The protest was provoked by a March 8 bomb in front of the clubhouse, which injured no one but shattered the windows of nearby homes and sent glass flying into a baby's crib.
"This place is like a shooting gallery," said one resident at a town meeting called to address the problem.
Saint-Nicolas Mayor Richard Blondin said the town would try to buy the Hell's Angels' house. But Blondin's solution was seen merely passing Saint-Nicolas' problem to another community.

After being pushed out of Montreal in the 1980s by city officials, the Hell's Angels built bunkers and houses reinforced with steel plates and concrete blocks in smaller Quebec communities such as Trois-Rivieres, Lennoxville, and Saint-Nicolas.

The upstart Rock Machine, a gang formed by former Hell's Angels members and rival bikers, has a clubhouse in east-end Montreal within sight of the provincial police headquarters, and another in Beauport, a Quebec City suburb.
In 1996, the biker conflict moved to Quebec City, a former French garrison town known by tourists for its fine restaurants, historic buildings and low crime rate.
Residents of the city's poorer lower town have since weathered dozens of bombings and shooting at bars and restaurants affiliated with the biker gangs.
Two weeks ago, a male bystander was shot as two masked gunmen shot and killed a suspected gang member in a lower town restaurant.
